tagline: The skin is the body's first line of defense, and the nurse is often the first to see it fail.
overview: Tissue integrity means intact skin, mucous membranes, cornea, and subcutaneous tissue that can protect, sense, regulate temperature, and repair itself. This concept covers normal skin structure and function, how to assess skin across all skin tones, infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic skin disorders, how wounds are classified and cared for in acute settings, the labs and nutrition that affect healing, nursing, collaborative, and pharmacologic therapies, and skin changes across the lifespan.

topics.title: Skin Structure & Function
topics.summary: The skin is the largest organ in the body. Its three layers work together to protect, sense, regulate temperature, remove wastes, and make vitamin D.

sections.heading: The integumentary system
sections.body: The integumentary system includes the skin, hair, nails, and glands. The skin is the largest organ, and it protects and maintains health. Tissue integrity is broader than skin alone: it means intact skin, mucous membranes, cornea, and subcutaneous tissue. Impaired tissue integrity is damage to the epidermis and/or dermis. It is influenced by internal factors (genetics, age, overall health) and external factors (activity, environment, injury). At-risk groups include older adults, clients with limited mobility, chronic illness, trauma, and invasive procedures.

sections.heading: Layers of the skin
bullets: Epidermis (outer layer). It is the barrier layer and has no blood vessels. Keratin makes it durable and water-resistant, and melanin protects against UV damage.
Dermis (middle layer, the “working layer”). It holds the blood vessels and nerve endings that support sensation, plus the sweat and oil (sebaceous) glands and hair follicles.

Subcutaneous tissue / hypodermis (innermost). Technically it is not skin, but it is vital for protection. It stores about half of the body's fat cells, insulates and cushions, and anchors the skin to underlying structures.

sections.heading: Functions of the skin
bullets: Protection against microorganisms and trauma. Intact skin also keeps body fluids in.
Sensation: touch, pain, pressure, and temperature.
Temperature regulation: blood vessels dilate to release heat and constrict to conserve it, and sweat glands cool the body by evaporation.
Removal of toxins through sweat.
Vitamin D synthesis from UV light. Less sun exposure, more melanin, and older age all reduce it.

sections.heading: Lifespan snapshot
sections.body: Infants have thinner skin that gives less protection. Adults have thicker, more hydrated skin. Older adults have thinner, less elastic skin.

table.caption: Skin layers at a glance
rows: Keratin (durable, water-resistant), melanin (UV protection); no blood vessels
An injury limited to the epidermis does not bleed
“Working layer”: vessels, nerve endings, sweat and oil glands, hair follicles
Damage here causes pain and bleeding; loss of sensation ↑ injury risk
Stores about half of the body's fat; insulates, cushions, anchors skin

pearls: Any break in the skin creates two immediate problems: a portal for infection and loss of fluid and heat.
The epidermis has no blood vessels. A wound that bleeds has reached at least the dermis.
When sensation is lost (for example, neuropathy), the client must replace feeling with looking: daily skin inspection and testing water temperature with a thermometer or an unaffected body part.
redFlags: Loss of skin over a large area. Watch for fluid loss, heat loss, and infection.

topics.title: Skin Assessment & Lesions
topics.summary: Accurate skin assessment across all skin tones depends on knowing where to look, how to palpate, and the right name for what you see.

sections.heading: General skin assessment
sections.body: Inspect in good (natural, if possible) light and compare both sides. Assess color, temperature, moisture, texture, edema, and lesions, and ask about itching, recent changes, sun exposure, new products, medications, and home remedies. Describe lesions by type, size, color, shape, distribution, and drainage.

sections.heading: Cultural considerations: assessing darker skin tones
sections.body: Skin color varies with melanin, which protects from UV damage, so assessment differs for light and dark skin tones. Rely on sites with little pigment and on palpation.
bullets: Pallor looks yellow-brown or ashen gray.
Cyanosis: check the nail beds, lips, and buccal mucosa.
Jaundice: check the palms and soles, not just the sclera.

Pressure injuries and inflammation are harder to detect. Look for darker, taut, shiny, or indurated areas. Check temperature, edema, and induration, and compare with nearby skin. Moistening the skin may help reveal changes.

After lesions heal, darker skin may show discoloration. It is also at risk for melasma (dark facial patches from sun). Some products (makeup, bleaching creams) can irritate the skin or interact with medications.

sections.heading: Classifying skin disorders
sections.body: Skin disorders are hard to classify because symptoms (itching, redness, inflammation) are often vague. Two common methods are acute vs chronic and by type: infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic.
bullets: Acute disorders are short-term with situational causes (bacterial infections, dermatitis). Treatment reduces inflammation and avoids triggers.
Chronic disorders are long-term or lifelong, with genetic or unknown causes (pigment changes, genetic skin conditions, psoriasis). Treatment aims for remission, not cure.
The skin can also reflect systemic disease. For example, dry skin with hair loss suggests hypothyroidism, and pinpoint bleeding spots (petechiae) can reflect a clotting problem.

sections.heading: Skin lesions
sections.body: Primary lesions arise from previously normal skin: macules, papules, nodules, vesicles, pustules, bullae, and wheals. Secondary lesions develop from primary lesions or trauma: crusts, scales, scars, keloids, fissures, ulcers, and erosions.

table.caption: Primary and secondary skin lesions
rows: Flat, nonpalpable color change, less than 1 cm
Raised, firm, deeper, larger than a papule
Clear-fluid-filled; vesicle less than 1 cm, bulla more than 1 cm
Transient, irregular, raised, itchy, edematous area
Loss of epidermis only / deeper loss into dermis or below
Fibrous tissue replacing damaged skin / overgrown scar extending beyond the wound
Healed incision / keloid on an earlobe

pearls: In darker skin, you often can't “see” redness. Palpate for warmth, induration, and edema, and compare with adjacent skin.
Pallor → conjunctivae and mucosa; cyanosis → nail beds, lips, buccal mucosa; jaundice → palms and soles, not just the sclera.
Document lesions by type, size (mm or cm), color, shape, distribution, and drainage. “Rash on arm” is not an assessment.
redFlags: Ashen gray lips and mucosa with a rapid pulse or low BP point to poor perfusion or oxygenation. Act, don't just document.
Raised wheals with hoarseness, wheezing, or throat tightness mean the reaction is affecting the airway.

topics.title: Infectious Skin Disorders
topics.summary: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites cause skin infections. The nurse recognizes them, prevents their spread, and teaches.

sections.heading: Causes and key points
bullets: Bacteria and viruses are the most common causes.
Fungal infections are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients (for example, clients receiving chemotherapy or with HIV/AIDS).
HPV (the virus that causes warts) increases cancer risk.
Prevention for everyone: hand hygiene, proper hygiene and skin care, and not sharing personal items (combs, hats, towels).

sections.heading: Bacterial: impetigo
sections.body: A contagious superficial bacterial infection, common in children. Vesicles and pustules break open and form honey-colored crusts, often around the nose and mouth. It spreads by direct contact, so use contact precautions and hand hygiene, gently wash crusts off with soap and water before applying the prescribed antibiotic, keep nails short, and don't share towels. Children usually stay out of school or child care until 24 hours after treatment starts.

sections.heading: Viral: chickenpox (varicella) and warts
bullets: Chickenpox: itchy vesicles in crops, with lesions in different stages at the same time. It is highly contagious, so use airborne + contact precautions until all lesions are crusted; only staff with documented immunity should care for the client. Relieve itching (cool baths, short nails) and use acetaminophen, not aspirin, for fever in children (Reye syndrome).
Herpes simplex and herpes zoster are among the most common skin conditions in the U.S. Their vesicles can be tested with a Tzanck test.
Warts (HPV) are common in children and adolescents and spread by touch, including picking or biting them.

sections.heading: Fungal: tinea (athlete's foot, ringworm)
sections.body: Fungi thrive in warm, moist areas. Athlete's foot causes itching, scaling, and cracked (fissured) skin between the toes. Ringworm is a ring-shaped scaly patch with central clearing. Diagnose with a KOH prep. Teach the client to dry between the toes, wear clean cotton socks and shower shoes in public showers, use the full course of antifungal, and not share towels, combs, or hats.

sections.heading: Parasitic: lice and scabies
bullets: Lice: itching, with nits attached to hair shafts near the scalp. Treat with an OTC pediculicide used exactly as labeled (no conditioner right before), comb out nits with a fine-tooth comb, wash bedding and hats in hot water and dry on high heat (or bag items that can't be washed), recheck the hair, and don't share combs, brushes, or hats. Insecticide sprays are not needed.

Scabies (a mite): intense itching, often worse at night, with small burrows in the finger webs and wrists. It spreads by close contact, so use contact precautions, treat the client and close contacts at the same time, and wash recently used bedding and clothing in hot water (or bag it).

pearls: Chickenpox: airborne + contact until ALL lesions are crusted. Assign only staff with documented immunity.
No aspirin for children with chickenpox or other viral illnesses (Reye syndrome).
Fungal infections are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients.
Lice and scabies spread through shared items and close contact. Teach clients not to share combs, hats, or towels.
redFlags: Any skin infection with fever and rapidly spreading redness, swelling, or drainage
A fungal skin infection in an immunocompromised client

topics.title: Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
topics.summary: Acne, eczema, burns, psoriasis, and dermatitis are inflammatory skin disorders. Many are itchy and visible, and they affect comfort, sleep, and self-image.

sections.heading: Contact dermatitis
bullets: Allergic contact dermatitis: an immune (delayed) reaction to an allergen the client has met before. The rash appears at the allergen site, may form vesicles or wheals, and is shaped like the item (a watchband, a jeans snap from nickel, streaks from poison ivy). Common allergens include metals, poison plants, latex, dyes, and perfumes. Confirm with patch testing.

Irritant contact dermatitis: direct damage from chemicals, soaps, or detergents. It is not immune-related, so it can occur on first exposure. The skin is red, dry, cracked, and burning where it was exposed.
Age considerations: infants have the strongest irritant response (for example, diaper dermatitis), adults have most allergic contact dermatitis, and older adults have slower, less intense reactions.
Care: identify and avoid the trigger, wash the skin after exposure, use cool compresses and moisturizers, and give prescribed topical corticosteroids and antihistamines for itching.

sections.heading: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
sections.body: A chronic, relapsing, very itchy inflammation caused by a weak skin barrier that loses moisture. In darker skin it may look darker brown, purple, or gray rather than red. Care: short lukewarm baths, a mild fragrance-free cleanser, pat dry and apply a thick moisturizer right away, cotton clothing, short nails, and avoiding triggers such as wool, fragrance, and heat. Prescription topical medicines treat flares. Scratching can lead to infection.

sections.heading: Psoriasis
sections.body: A chronic immune-related disorder in which skin cells build up too quickly, forming well-defined red plaques with silvery-white scale, often on the elbows, knees, and scalp. In darker skin, plaques may look violet or dark brown with gray scale. There is no cure, so treatment (prescription topical and oral medicines) aims for remission. Teach the client to moisturize, avoid injuring or scratching the skin, and manage stress.

sections.heading: Acne
sections.body: Puberty hormones increase sebum and sweating, so clogged follicles and bacteria produce comedones, papules, and pustules. Acne affects about 50 million Americans each year, including about 85% of people aged 12–24. Teach the client to wash gently twice a day, not pick or squeeze, and use non-comedogenic products. Darker skin is prone to dark spots after acne heals, so early treatment matters.

No; can occur on first exposure

pearls: A rash in the exact shape of a watch, ring, or jeans button suggests allergic contact dermatitis.
Eczema: lukewarm bath, pat dry, moisturize right away.
Chronic disorders such as psoriasis are controlled (remission), not cured.
Poison ivy rash is not spread by blister fluid. Wash the plant oil off the skin, clothing, and tools.
redFlags: Hives with wheezing, hoarseness, or throat tightness after an allergen exposure (airway involvement)
Scratched eczema or dermatitis that becomes red, warm, swollen, or starts draining pus (secondary infection)

topics.title: Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
topics.summary: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the U.S. Many skin disorders, including most skin cancer, can be prevented or caught early with simple measures.

sections.heading: Neoplastic (cancerous) disorders
bullets: Basal cell carcinoma: the most common type. Often a pearly or waxy bump on sun-exposed skin that may bleed or not heal. It grows slowly and rarely spreads.

Squamous cell carcinoma: a rough, scaly, crusted bump or sore on sun-exposed skin (face, lips, ears, hands). It can spread. Rough, scaly sun-damage patches (actinic keratoses) can become squamous cell carcinoma.

Malignant melanoma: the most serious type. It arises from pigment cells and can spread early. Teach the ABCDE warning signs: Asymmetry, irregular Border, varied Color, Diameter larger than about 6 mm, and Evolving (changing). Any changing mole should be checked, whatever its size.

sections.heading: Risk factors
bullets: Genetics and family history increase risk (for example, a parent with melanoma).
Lighter skin has a higher risk of UV damage, and blistering sunburns add risk. Clients with darker skin can still get skin cancer, so all clients are at risk regardless of skin tone.
Extrinsic aging from UV, smoking, pollution, and chemicals causes precancerous changes.
Some medications (steroids, antibiotics such as doxycycline, chemotherapy, antifungals) may thin the skin or increase sun sensitivity.

sections.heading: Health promotion and modifiable risk factors
bullets: Sun protection: sunscreen (broad-spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, reapplied about every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating), hats, protective clothing, and shade. Avoid tanning beds.
Keep skin clean, dry, and moisturized. Avoid excessive cleansing, which dries the skin, and use moisturizers regularly.
Cover and care for wounds to reduce infection risk.
Avoid irritants and allergens: chemicals, dyes, perfumes, poison plants, latex, and metals.
Don't share personal items such as combs and hats.

Special groups: children need proper diaper care with frequent changes; chronic illness (diabetes, HIV/AIDS, obesity, poor circulation) increases risk; poor nutrition causes skin changes and delayed healing.

sections.heading: Skin screenings
bullets: Self-examinations help clients learn what their normal skin looks like and recognize changes early. Focus on sun-exposed areas (face, neck, ears, scalp, arms, legs) and also check the trunk, chest, and feet. Use mirrors or a partner for hard-to-see areas.
Professional exams: a full skin inspection by a dermatologist or provider, which may include biopsy, cultures, or patch testing.

pearls: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer. Melanoma is the most serious.
“E” (evolving) matters most: report any mole that is changing, even if it is small.
Sun protection is for every skin tone.
Clients on photosensitizing medicines (for example, doxycycline) need extra sun protection.
redFlags: A mole that is changing, bleeding, or meets the ABCDE criteria. Refer for evaluation and biopsy.
A sore or scaly, crusted spot that bleeds or doesn't heal

topics.title: Wound Types & Classification
topics.summary: Classifying a wound by cause, skin integrity, contamination, and depth predicts infection risk and shapes acute wound care.

sections.heading: Types of wounds
bullets: Intentional wounds are created for therapy: surgery, venipuncture.
Unintentional wounds are accidental: fractures, lacerations.
Closed wounds: the skin is intact but the tissue underneath is injured (contusion). They can still hide bleeding and swelling.
Open wounds: the skin or mucous membrane is broken, which gives microorganisms a way in.

sections.heading: Classification by contamination
bullets: Clean: closed, no infection, sterile environment maintained (for example, a hernia repair).
Clean-contaminated: a controlled surgical entry into the GI, GU, or respiratory tract (for example, an elective bowel or gallbladder surgery).
Contaminated: an open, fresh accidental wound, a major break in sterile technique, spillage from the GI tract, or inflammation present.
Dirty/Infected: purulent drainage, dead tissue, or a clinical infection already present (for example, an old traumatic wound with pus, or a ruptured appendix).

sections.heading: Classification by depth
bullets: Partial-thickness: loss of the epidermis and part of the dermis. Heals by regeneration, usually with little or no scar.
Full-thickness: loss of all skin layers, possibly extending to muscle or bone. Requires connective tissue repair and leaves a scar.

sections.heading: Wound care in acute settings
bullets: Control bleeding: after hand hygiene and gloves, apply firm direct pressure and elevate.
Prevent infection: once bleeding is controlled, clean with normal saline and cover with a dressing.
Manage pain and swelling: apply ice (wrapped in a cloth, not directly on the skin).
Assess for shock: rapid pulse, cool clammy skin, low BP, restlessness. Report these right away.
Treated wounds: at each dressing change, monitor healing and check for drainage, pain, and signs of infection (increasing redness, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, odor, fever).

table.caption: Wound classification by contamination
rows: No GI, GU, or respiratory tract entered; no infection; sterile technique maintained
GI, GU, or respiratory tract entered under controlled conditions
Open, fresh accidental wound; major sterile break; spillage; inflammation
Purulent drainage, dead tissue, clinical infection present

pearls: Tract entered on purpose and under control = clean-contaminated. A fresh accident or spillage = contaminated. Pus or dead tissue already there = dirty/infected.
Pressure and elevation first. Clean and cover only after bleeding is controlled.
Partial-thickness wounds regenerate. Full-thickness wounds scar.
redFlags: Bleeding that soaks through dressings despite direct pressure, or signs of shock (rapid pulse, clammy skin, low BP)
A closed wound (contusion) with tense, enlarging swelling, especially in a client taking an anticoagulant

topics.title: Diagnostics, Labs & Nursing Care
topics.summary: The right test identifies the cause of a skin problem. Labs, nutrition, hygiene, and infection prevention decide whether tissue can heal.

sections.heading: Diagnostic tests
bullets: Skin biopsy: identifies whether a lesion is benign or cancerous. Afterward, keep the site clean and covered and watch for bleeding and signs of infection.
Cultures of tissue, drainage, exudate, or serum identify infection and guide antibiotic choice. Collect them before the first antibiotic dose when possible.
KOH prep: detects fungal infection (for example, tinea).
Tzanck test: tests viral lesions (vesicles from herpes viruses).
Wood lamp exam: an ultraviolet (black light) exam in a darkened room. Some fungal infections and pigment loss show up under the light. The skin should be free of lotions and makeup.
Immunofluorescence studies: detect antibodies in skin samples (used for some autoimmune skin diseases).

Allergy tests: scratch, intradermal, and patch tests. Patch tests (for contact allergy) stay on and dry for about 48 hours, and the skin is read again a few days later because the reaction is delayed.
Carrier studies: nasal cultures for clients with repeated infections, to see whether they carry the bacteria (for example, Staphylococcus aureus).

sections.heading: Laboratory data and wound healing
bullets: WBC ↓: poor infection defense and delayed healing. A low WBC can also hide the usual signs of infection.
Hemoglobin ↓: less oxygen delivered to the tissues.
Coagulation studies: prolonged times → excessive bleeding. Hypercoagulability → clotting and poor wound perfusion.
Albumin less than 3.5 g/dL: poor nutrition, ↑ risk of infection and delayed healing.
Wound cultures: confirm infection and guide antibiotic choice.
Chronic illness such as diabetes also slows healing, so high blood glucose in a client with a wound needs follow-up.

sections.heading: Independent nursing interventions
bullets: Goals: control disease, prevent infection, and promote healing.
Assess home remedies, because some may hinder healing.
Hygiene: adults bathe daily; children and older adults every other day. Avoid harsh soap and use mild or liquid cleansers. Moisturize after bathing.
Teach comfort and skin-protection strategies.

sections.heading: Infection prevention, exercise, and nutrition
bullets: Infection prevention: proper wound cleaning and dressing, hand hygiene before and after wound care, safe disposal of soiled dressings, and teaching the signs of infection (redness, swelling, drainage, necrosis).
Exercise promotes blood flow and helps prevent pressure injuries.

Nutrition supports healing: ↑ calories, protein, and vitamins A and C. Encourage whole grains, vegetables, citrus, dairy, and lean proteins. Offer small frequent meals or supplements if intake is poor, and consult the dietitian.

table.caption: Matching the test to the question
rows: Changing mole, pearly bump that bleeds

pearls: Albumin less than 3.5 g/dL = risk for infection and delayed healing.
Get the culture before the first antibiotic dose.
KOH = fungus. Tzanck = virus. Patch test = contact allergy. Biopsy = cancer.
Hand hygiene before AND after wound care, and dispose of soiled dressings safely.
redFlags: A client with a wound, albumin less than 3.5 g/dL, and poor intake needs a dietitian referral and a nutrition plan now.
Fever, spreading redness, purulent drainage, or new odor from a wound
Bleeding from a wound in a client with prolonged clotting times

topics.title: Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
topics.summary: Skin care is a team effort. Most skin medicines are topical, and safe use depends on applying them correctly and watching for irritation and interactions.

sections.heading: Collaborative therapies
sections.body: An interprofessional team improves outcomes through better communication and fewer complications. Key members include nurses, UAPs, wound care nurses, case managers, health care providers, dermatologists, oncologists, and surgeons.

sections.heading: Pharmacologic therapy
bullets: OTC medicines treat minor acne, lice, and sunburn.

Benzoyl peroxide: the first-line acne treatment. It kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Expect some dryness and peeling; start with a thin layer, use gently, and know that it can bleach towels, clothing, and hair.
Salicylic acid: exfoliates (removes dead skin cells) and reduces inflammation.

Prescription medicines (oral and topical) treat eczema, psoriasis, and dermatitis. Topical corticosteroids are common: apply a thin layer with gloves, don't cover with an occlusive dressing unless prescribed, and avoid stronger products on the face and skin folds. Long-term use can thin the skin.
Skin tone differences: darker skin is more prone to inflammation and may need combination therapy (for example, chemical peels, microdermabrasion).

sections.heading: Nonpharmacologic therapy
bullets: Proper wound care, dressing changes, and nutrition.
Burns: daily debridement and sterile dressings.
Pressure injuries: care varies by stage and facility protocol.
Severe wounds: negative pressure wound therapy (vacuum devices).

sections.heading: Complementary approaches
sections.body: Aloe vera, chamomile, and evening primrose oil may soothe irritation and promote healing, but the evidence is limited. Ask every client about them, and monitor for drug interactions and allergies. For example, evening primrose oil may add to the bleeding risk of anticoagulants, and a product that burns or stings should be stopped.

table.caption: Common skin therapies
rows: Kills bacteria, unplugs ducts; dryness expected; bleaches fabric
Use exactly as labeled; comb out nits; recheck hair
Thin layer; no occlusion unless ordered; report skin thinning
Aloe vera, chamomile, evening primrose oil
Limited evidence; check for allergies and drug interactions

pearls: Benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Salicylic acid exfoliates and reduces inflammation.
Topical corticosteroid: a thin layer only, and no occlusion unless ordered.
Always ask about complementary products. “Natural” does not mean free of interactions.
redFlags: Thin, shiny, easily bruised skin where a topical steroid has been used for a long time
A complementary product used together with an anticoagulant, or one that causes burning, rash, or swelling

topics.title: Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Newborns, children, adolescents, pregnant clients, and older adults each have expected skin findings. The nurse knows which ones are normal and which need follow-up.

sections.heading: Newborns
bullets: Vernix caseosa is a white, cheesy coating that protects the skin. It doesn't need to be scrubbed off.
Thinner skin means more heat loss and a higher risk of absorbing products put on the skin, so use products sparingly.

Common, harmless findings: milia (tiny white bumps on the nose and chin), neonatal acne, erythema toxicum (blotchy red spots with small pale-yellow or white centers that come and go and fade on their own), and birthmarks (for example, blue-gray patches over the lower back and buttocks in darker-skinned infants, which should be documented so they aren't mistaken for bruises).

sections.heading: Children
sections.body: Children have a larger body surface area, so they lose more fluid and heat. Common infections are fungal (tinea), viral (warts, varicella), and parasitic (lice, scabies). Other conditions: fifth disease (bright red “slapped cheek” rash, then a lacy rash on the arms and legs), roseola (several days of high fever, then a rash as the fever breaks), and pityriasis rosea (one larger oval “herald patch,” then smaller oval patches on the trunk). Diaper care: change diapers often and keep the skin clean and dry.

sections.heading: Adolescents
sections.body: Puberty hormones increase sebum and sweating. Common disorders are acne, dermatitis, psoriasis, fungal infections, and warts. Skin problems strongly affect body image, so address feelings as well as treatment.

sections.heading: Pregnancy
sections.body: Common changes are hyperpigmentation (for example, a dark line down the abdomen and darker patches on the face), stretch marks, and pruritus (itching). Atopic eruption of pregnancy (AEP) is an itchy, eczema-like rash that resolves after delivery.

sections.heading: Older adults and the aging process
bullets: Intrinsic aging starts at about age 20: slower exfoliation, ↓ moisture, ↓ fat cells. In the 30s skin becomes dull and thin; in the 40s ↓ collagen causes wrinkles; after menopause, ↓ estrogen makes skin thinner and drier.
Extrinsic aging comes from UV, pollution, smoking, and chemicals and causes skin thickening, precancerous changes, and wrinkling.

Normal changes: thinner, less elastic skin; wrinkles and sagging; slower healing; ↓ sebaceous glands → dry skin; ↓ subcutaneous fat → less cushioning and poor temperature regulation; paler, translucent skin (fewer melanocytes); age spots; fragile vessels (senile purpura); fat loss in the face and hands with gain in the thighs and abdomen.
Functional changes: ↓ sensation, ↑ healing time, ↑ injury risk, ↓ temperature regulation.

Nursing care: bathe every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser, pat dry, and moisturize; lift with a draw sheet rather than dragging; pad bed rails and wheelchair arms; avoid adhesive tape on fragile skin; long sleeves protect the arms.

pearls: Vernix, milia, neonatal acne, and erythema toxicum are expected newborn findings. Reassure the parents.
Newborn skin absorbs products easily and loses heat quickly.
Pregnancy: hyperpigmentation, stretch marks, and itching are common; AEP resolves after delivery.
Older adults: no hot water, no vigorous rubbing, no adhesive tape on fragile skin, and never drag the client up in bed.
redFlags: Bruises in different stages of healing in protected areas (inner arms, trunk) that don't match the history, at any age
A newborn or child whose rash comes with fever, poor feeding, or lethargy

flashcards.front: Which skin layer contains blood vessels, nerve endings, and sweat and oil glands?
flashcards.back: The dermis, the “working layer.” The epidermis has no blood vessels.

flashcards.front: Name five functions of the skin.
flashcards.back: Protection (microorganisms and trauma), sensation, temperature regulation, removing toxins through sweat, and vitamin D synthesis from UV light.

flashcards.front: What does the subcutaneous tissue do?
flashcards.back: Stores about half of the body's fat, insulates and cushions, and anchors skin to underlying structures. It is not technically skin.

flashcards.front: Where do you assess pallor, cyanosis, and jaundice in a client with dark skin?
flashcards.back: Pallor: looks yellow-brown or ashen gray. Cyanosis: nail beds, lips, buccal mucosa. Jaundice: palms and soles, not just the sclera.

flashcards.front: How do you detect inflammation or early pressure damage in darker skin?
flashcards.back: Look for darker, taut, shiny, or indurated areas. Check temperature, edema, and induration. Moistening the skin may help reveal changes.

flashcards.front: Primary vs secondary lesion?
flashcards.back: Primary arises from normal skin (macule, papule, nodule, vesicle, pustule, bulla, wheal). Secondary develops from a primary lesion or trauma (crust, scale, scar, keloid, fissure, ulcer, erosion).

flashcards.front: Acute vs chronic skin disorders?
flashcards.back: Acute: short-term, situational (bacterial infection, dermatitis); reduce inflammation, avoid triggers. Chronic: long-term or lifelong; treatment = remission, not cure.

flashcards.front: Give an example of each type of infectious skin disorder.
flashcards.back: Bacterial → impetigo. Fungal → athlete's foot. Viral → chickenpox. Parasitic → lice.

flashcards.front: Honey-colored crusts around a child's nose and mouth?
flashcards.back: Impetigo (bacterial). Contact precautions, gently wash crusts off, give the prescribed antibiotic, don't share towels, and keep nails short.

flashcards.front: Isolation for chickenpox?
flashcards.back: Airborne + contact until all lesions are crusted. Assign only staff with documented immunity. No aspirin for children (Reye syndrome).

flashcards.front: Which clients are most endangered by fungal skin infections?
flashcards.back: Immunocompromised clients (for example, those receiving chemotherapy or with HIV/AIDS).

flashcards.front: Allergic vs irritant contact dermatitis?
flashcards.back: Allergic: immune reaction at the allergen site, shaped like the item, with vesicles or wheals; mostly adults; patch test. Irritant: chemicals, soap, detergent; not immune-related; strongest in infants.

flashcards.front: Classic psoriasis lesion and treatment goal?
flashcards.back: Well-defined red plaques with silvery-white scale on the elbows, knees, and scalp. It is chronic, so the goal is remission, not cure.

flashcards.front: Bathing and skin care for eczema?
flashcards.back: Short lukewarm bath, mild fragrance-free cleanser, pat dry and moisturize right away. Avoid wool, fragrance, and heat.

flashcards.front: Name the three neoplastic skin disorders. Which is most serious?
flashcards.back: Basal cell carcinoma (most common), squamous cell carcinoma, and malignant melanoma (most serious).

flashcards.front: ABCDE of melanoma?
flashcards.back: Asymmetry, Border irregular, Color variation, Diameter larger than about 6 mm, Evolving (any change).

flashcards.front: Where should a skin self-exam focus?
flashcards.back: Sun-exposed areas (face, neck, ears, scalp, arms, legs), plus the trunk, chest, and feet.

flashcards.front: Key preventive measures for skin disorders?
flashcards.back: Sun protection (sunscreen, hats, protective clothing), proper hygiene and skin care, keep skin clean, dry, and moisturized, avoid irritants and allergens, and don't share personal items.

flashcards.front: The 4 wound classes by contamination?
flashcards.back: Clean (no tract entered, sterile), Clean-contaminated (controlled entry into GI, GU, or respiratory tract), Contaminated (open, fresh, major sterile break, spillage), Dirty/Infected (pus, dead tissue, clinical infection).

flashcards.front: Intentional vs unintentional? Closed vs open?
flashcards.back: Intentional: created for therapy (surgery, venipuncture). Unintentional: accidental. Closed: skin intact, tissue injured (contusion). Open: skin or mucous membrane broken.

flashcards.front: Partial vs full-thickness healing?
flashcards.back: Partial (epidermis and part of dermis) heals by regeneration. Full (all skin layers, may reach muscle or bone) needs connective tissue repair.

flashcards.front: Acute care for an untreated wound?
flashcards.back: Pressure and elevate to control bleeding → clean with saline and cover → ice for pain and swelling → assess for shock (rapid pulse, clammy skin, low BP).

flashcards.front: Albumin value that signals risk for delayed healing?
flashcards.back: Less than 3.5 g/dL: poor nutrition, ↑ infection risk, delayed healing.

flashcards.front: KOH prep, Tzanck test, patch test, biopsy: what does each detect?
flashcards.back: KOH: fungus. Tzanck: viral lesions. Patch test: contact allergy. Biopsy: benign vs cancerous.

flashcards.front: How do WBC, hemoglobin, and coagulation results affect healing?
flashcards.back: ↓ WBC: poor infection defense. ↓ Hemoglobin: less oxygen to tissue. Prolonged clotting: bleeding; hypercoagulability: clotting and poor perfusion.

flashcards.front: Nutrients that support tissue repair?
flashcards.back: ↑ Calories and protein, vitamins A and C. Whole grains, vegetables, citrus, dairy, lean proteins; small frequent meals or supplements if needed.

flashcards.front: Benzoyl peroxide vs salicylic acid?
flashcards.back: Benzoyl peroxide: first-line acne treatment; kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Salicylic acid: exfoliates and reduces inflammation.

flashcards.front: How to apply a topical corticosteroid?
flashcards.back: Thin layer with gloves, no occlusion unless ordered, avoid stronger products on the face and skin folds. Long-term use can thin the skin.

flashcards.front: Complementary skin therapies and the nurse's role?
flashcards.back: Aloe vera, chamomile, evening primrose oil may soothe irritation, but evidence is limited. Ask about use and monitor for drug interactions and allergies.

flashcards.front: Expected newborn skin findings?
flashcards.back: Vernix caseosa, milia, neonatal acne, erythema toxicum, and birthmarks. Thin skin → heat loss and ↑ absorption.

flashcards.front: Intrinsic vs extrinsic aging?
flashcards.back: Intrinsic: natural, starts about age 20 (↓ moisture, ↓ fat, ↓ collagen in the 40s, thinner after menopause). Extrinsic: UV, pollution, smoking, chemicals → thickening, precancerous changes, wrinkles.

flashcards.front: Why bathe older adults every other day with lukewarm water?
flashcards.back: ↓ Sebaceous glands → dry, fragile skin. Frequent hot bathing strips oils and causes dryness, itching, and skin tears.

questions.stem: A client has a superficial abrasion that is oozing small amounts of blood and is painful to touch. The nurse recognizes that the injury has reached which skin layer?
options: The stratum corneum of the epidermis only
The dermis, which contains blood vessels and nerve endings
The subcutaneous layer, which stores adipose tissue
The basal layer of the epidermis, which contains capillaries
optionRationales: The stratum corneum is dead keratinized cells with no vessels or nerves, so injury limited to it would not bleed or hurt.
Correct. The epidermis is avascular. Bleeding and pain mean the injury has reached the dermis, where the blood vessels and sensory nerve endings are.
The subcutaneous layer is fat and connective tissue. A superficial abrasion does not usually reach it.
The basal layer has no capillaries. The epidermis is nourished by diffusion from the dermis.
questions.rationale: The epidermis contains no blood vessels. Any wound that bleeds has reached at least the dermis, the “working layer” that holds vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles.
questions.takeaway: If it bleeds, it has reached the dermis.

questions.hintContent: Think about what intact skin prevents minute to minute: microbial entry and evaporative water and heat loss.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a priority item. Rank options by Maslow and ABCs. Physiological threats to circulation outrank psychosocial or long-term concerns.

questions.stem: A client is admitted after losing a large area of epidermis and dermis over the back and legs. Based on the normal functions of the skin, which nursing problem is the priority?
options: Impaired vitamin D synthesis from reduced UV absorption in the damaged skin
Disturbed body image related to visible skin loss on the back and legs
Decreased tactile sensation and pain perception over the affected areas
Fluid volume deficit and infection from loss of the protective barrier
optionRationales: Vitamin D synthesis is a real skin function, but losing it is not an immediate threat to life.
Body image matters, but psychosocial needs come after physiological threats.
Loss of sensation is a safety concern, but it is less urgent than fluid loss and infection.
Correct. The skin is the barrier against microorganisms and evaporative water loss. Large skin loss quickly leads to fluid loss, heat loss, and infection, which threaten circulation and life.
questions.rationale: Protection (from infection and fluid loss) and thermoregulation are the skin functions whose loss threatens life. Maslow and ABC priorities place physiological threats, especially circulation and fluid volume, above psychosocial and long-term concerns.
questions.takeaway: Large skin loss = fluid loss + infection + heat loss. These are the immediate threats.

questions.hintContent: Recall which layer stores fat and what fat does for the body.
questions.hintStrategy: Match each finding to the layer that performs that function, then choose only the findings tied to fat loss.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client in a long-term care facility has the following findings. Which findings are best explained by age-related changes in the subcutaneous tissue? Select all that apply.
options: Reports feeling cold in a 72°F (22°C) room and needs extra blankets
Did not notice a burn from a heating pad left on the lower back
Has very dry, flaky, itchy skin on the shins
Skin appears paler and more translucent than in earlier photos
Has little cushioning over the sacrum and heels
Has hollowed cheeks and thin, bony-looking hands
optionRationales: Correct. Loss of subcutaneous fat removes insulation, so older adults regulate body temperature poorly and feel cold in rooms that are comfortable for others.
Incorrect. Missing a burn reflects decreased sensation from fewer nerve endings in the dermis, the "working layer" of the skin.
Incorrect. Dry, flaky skin reflects fewer sebaceous (oil) glands, which are located in the dermis.
Incorrect. Paler, translucent skin reflects fewer melanocytes in the epidermis.
Correct. The subcutaneous layer stores fat and cushions underlying structures. Its loss leaves bony areas poorly padded and at risk for injury.
Correct. Fat loss in the face and hands is a normal age-related change in the subcutaneous tissue.
questions.rationale: The subcutaneous tissue stores about half of the body's fat and helps cushion and insulate. With aging, subcutaneous fat decreases, especially in the face and hands, which causes less cushioning over bony areas and poor thermoregulation. Decreased sensation and dry skin reflect dermal changes (fewer nerve endings and sebaceous glands), and paler, translucent skin reflects fewer melanocytes in the epidermis.
questions.takeaway: Less subcutaneous fat = less cushioning, less insulation, hollowed face and hands.

questions.stem: A client with deeply pigmented skin and a COPD exacerbation has an SpO2 of 86% on 2 L/min nasal cannula and is increasingly short of breath. The nurse wants to assess for central cyanosis. Which area should the nurse inspect?
options: The skin of the forehead and cheeks
The lips and buccal (oral) mucosa
The skin over the sternum
The dorsal surface of the hands
optionRationales: Heavily pigmented facial skin hides the bluish or gray tint of cyanosis.
Correct. In dark skin, cyanosis is assessed in the nail beds, lips, and buccal mucosa, where there is little melanin. The mouth also reflects central oxygenation.
The skin over the sternum is pigmented, so a color change would be hard to see there.
The back of the hand is pigmented and shows peripheral, not central, changes.
questions.rationale: In darker skin, color changes are best seen where melanin is minimal. The slides list the nail beds, lips, and buccal mucosa for cyanosis. The lips and oral mucosa also reflect central oxygenation.
questions.takeaway: Dark skin: assess cyanosis in the nail beds, lips, and buccal mucosa.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing the sacrum of a client with dark brown skin who has been on bed rest for 3 days. Which techniques will help the nurse detect early tissue damage? Select all that apply.
options: Palpate the area for warmth compared with surrounding skin
Check for induration, edema, or a boggy feel
Inspect for areas that look darker, taut, or shiny
Rely on the presence of blanchable redness
Assess the area under overhead fluorescent light only
Lightly moisten the skin to make color changes easier to see
optionRationales: Correct. Warmth (or coolness) compared with adjacent skin is an early sign of inflammation or tissue damage that doesn't depend on color.
Correct. Induration, edema, and bogginess are palpable changes that reveal damage melanin may hide.
Correct. In darker skin, inflammation often looks darker (purple or maroon), taut, shiny, or indurated rather than red.
Incorrect. Redness and blanching may be impossible to see in dark skin. Relying on them leads to missed injury.
Incorrect. Natural or halogen light is preferred. Fluorescent light can give skin a bluish cast and hide changes.
Correct. Slightly moistening the skin can make subtle color and sheen changes easier to see.
questions.rationale: Detecting erythema by eye is unreliable in darkly pigmented skin. The nurse compensates by palpating for temperature, induration, and edema, looking for darker, shiny, or taut areas, using good natural light, and comparing with adjacent skin.
questions.takeaway: In dark skin, feel for warmth and induration. Don't wait to see redness.

questions.stem: Four hours after abdominal surgery, a client with dark skin is restless. Vital signs: HR 122/min, BP 92/58 mm Hg, RR 24/min, SpO2 93%. Which assessment finding requires the most immediate follow-up?
options: Hyperpigmented macules on the forearms from a previous rash
Dry, flaking skin on both lower legs
Ashen-gray lips and pale conjunctivae
A 2-cm keloid on the right earlobe
optionRationales: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is common after healed lesions in darker skin and is not urgent.
Dry skin (xerosis) is a comfort and skin-care issue, not an acute threat.

Correct. Ashen-gray color and pale conjunctivae are how pallor and cyanosis look in dark skin. With tachycardia, hypotension, and restlessness after surgery, they suggest hemorrhage or hypovolemic shock and need immediate action.
Keloids are more common in darker skin and are a chronic cosmetic finding.
questions.rationale: In dark skin, pallor looks ashen gray (or yellow-brown), and changes are best seen in the lips, mucosa, and conjunctivae. With abnormal vital signs, this points to impaired perfusion, an ABC priority.
questions.takeaway: Ashen gray + tachycardia + hypotension in dark skin = shock until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: The nurse notes several raised lesions on a child's trunk that are filled with clear fluid and measure about 0.5 cm each. How should the nurse document these lesions?
options: Vesicles
Pustules
Bullae
Wheals
optionRationales: Correct. A vesicle is a circumscribed, elevated, clear-fluid-filled primary lesion less than 1 cm, as seen in varicella or herpes.
Pustules contain purulent (cloudy, yellow) fluid, not clear fluid.
Bullae are clear-fluid-filled lesions larger than 1 cm.
Wheals are transient, edematous, irregular raised areas without a fluid-filled cavity, such as hives.
questions.rationale: Primary lesions are named by content and size. Clear fluid <1 cm is a vesicle, and >1 cm is a bulla. Pus-filled lesions are pustules.
questions.takeaway: Vesicle <1 cm, bulla >1 cm, and pustule = pus.

questions.hintContent: Ask whether each lesion is the first thing to appear on normal skin or a change that develops afterward.
questions.hintStrategy: Name each lesion first (macule, crust, wheal, and so on), then sort it.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old is seen in the clinic for several skin complaints, and the nurse documents the findings below. Which findings should the nurse document as primary lesions? Select all that apply.
options: Flat, brown, nonpalpable freckle 4 mm in diameter
Dried honey-colored exudate over a lesion
Transient raised, itchy hive after a bee sting
Linear crack in the skin between the toes
Pus-filled raised lesion on the chin
Thin, pale line of healed tissue from an old cut on the knee
optionRationales: Correct. A flat, nonpalpable color change smaller than 1 cm is a macule, a primary lesion.
Incorrect. Dried exudate is a crust, a secondary lesion that forms from a primary lesion.
Correct. A transient, raised, itchy area of edema is a wheal, a primary lesion.
Incorrect. A linear crack in the skin is a fissure, a secondary lesion.
Correct. A raised lesion filled with pus is a pustule, a primary lesion.
Incorrect. A scar is a secondary lesion that replaces damaged tissue after healing.
questions.rationale: Primary lesions arise directly from disease in previously normal skin: macules, papules, nodules, vesicles, pustules, bullae, and wheals. Secondary lesions develop from primary lesions or from scratching, injury, or healing: crusts, scales, scars, keloids, fissures, ulcers, and erosions.
questions.takeaway: Primary = first appearance (macule, wheal, pustule). Secondary = change over time (crust, fissure, scar).

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client reports dry, rough skin that lotions don't help, thinning hair, brittle nails, weight gain, constipation, and always feeling cold. HR 56/min. Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate the provider will order?
options: A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings
A patch test on the upper back
A thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level
A Wood lamp examination of the skin
optionRationales: Incorrect. A KOH preparation identifies fungal infection. The client has no scaly, ring-shaped lesions.
Incorrect. Patch testing identifies allergens in allergic contact dermatitis. It does not explain weight gain, cold intolerance, and bradycardia.
Correct. Dry skin and hair loss with weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and bradycardia suggest hypothyroidism, a systemic disease reflected in the skin. A TSH level screens for it.
Incorrect. A Wood lamp examines pigment changes and some infections. It does not evaluate systemic causes of dry skin.
questions.rationale: The skin can reflect systemic disease. Dry, rough skin, thinning hair, and brittle nails together with weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and a slow heart rate point to hypothyroidism rather than a primary skin disorder. The nurse anticipates a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level.
questions.takeaway: Dry skin + hair loss + cold intolerance + weight gain → think hypothyroidism → TSH.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth and is prescribed an antibiotic ointment. Which statement by the parent indicates the teaching was effective?
options: “I'll gently wash the crusts off with soap and water before applying the ointment.”
“My child can go back to kindergarten tomorrow since the rash isn't itchy.”
“The whole family can keep sharing bath towels as long as we wash them weekly.”
“I'll cover the sores tightly with plastic wrap overnight so they heal faster.”
optionRationales: Correct. Gently removing the crusts with soap and water lets the topical antibiotic reach the bacteria and reduces the bacterial load.
Impetigo is highly contagious. The child should stay home until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics, whether or not the rash itches.
Towels, washcloths, and linens should not be shared. They spread staph and strep.
Occlusive plastic wrap traps moisture and is not part of impetigo care. It can worsen maceration and spread.
questions.rationale: Impetigo is a contagious bacterial skin infection that spreads by direct contact. Care: gently remove crusts, apply the prescribed antibiotic, keep nails short, don't share personal items, wash hands, and keep the child out of school or child care until 24 hours after treatment starts.
questions.takeaway: Impetigo: remove crusts gently, apply the prescribed antibiotic, share nothing, stay home until 24 hours of treatment.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with type 2 diabetes and obesity asks how to keep the skin healthy. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the skin clean and dry, especially in skin folds and between the toes
Apply a moisturizer regularly, such as after bathing
Scrub the skin with antibacterial soap several times a day to prevent infection
Cover any cut or scrape and watch it for signs of infection
Choose fragrance-free and dye-free soaps and laundry products
Share towels only with family members who live in the same home
optionRationales: Correct. Clean, dry skin resists infection. Moist skin folds favor fungal growth.
Correct. Regular moisturizing keeps the skin barrier intact and prevents dry, cracked skin.
Incorrect. Excessive cleansing dries the skin and damages the barrier. Use a mild cleanser.
Correct. Covering and caring for wounds reduces infection risk, which is higher in clients with diabetes and obesity.
Correct. Dyes and perfumes are common irritants and allergens.
Incorrect. Personal items such as towels, combs, and hats should not be shared, even at home.
questions.rationale: Chronic illnesses such as diabetes and obesity increase the risk of skin problems. Modifiable risk factors include keeping the skin clean, dry, and moisturized, covering and caring for wounds, avoiding irritants and allergens (chemicals, dyes, perfumes), avoiding excessive cleansing, and not sharing personal items.
questions.takeaway: Clean, dry, moisturized skin; covered wounds; no irritants; no excessive washing; no sharing.

questions.stem: A client has a cluster of painful, fluid-filled vesicles on a red base on the upper lip. The provider wants to confirm whether the lesions are caused by a virus. Which test should the nurse anticipate?
options: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings
Patch testing on the upper back
Wood lamp examination
Tzanck test of fluid and cells from a vesicle
optionRationales: A KOH prep detects fungal infection, not a virus.
Patch testing identifies contact allergens, not infection.
A Wood lamp shows fluorescence of some fungal infections and pigment changes. It does not identify a viral cause of vesicles.
Correct. The Tzanck test is used for viral lesions. Scrapings from the base of a vesicle show cell changes caused by herpes viruses.
questions.rationale: Each skin test has a target. The Tzanck test is used for viral lesions (vesicles from herpes viruses), KOH for fungi, patch testing for contact allergy, the Wood lamp for fluorescence (some fungal infections, pigment loss), and biopsy for benign vs cancerous tissue.
questions.takeaway: Tzanck = viral vesicles. KOH = fungus. Patch test = contact allergy.

questions.stem: The charge nurse is making assignments on a pediatric unit. A child with active varicella is admitted to an airborne isolation room. Which staff member is most appropriate to assign to this child?
options: An RN who is 14 weeks pregnant and unsure of her varicella history
An RN who recently finished chemotherapy for breast cancer
A float LPN who has never had chickenpox or the varicella vaccine
An RN who had chickenpox as a child and has documented immunity
optionRationales: Pregnant staff without proven immunity should not care for varicella clients. Congenital varicella syndrome and severe maternal pneumonia are risks.
An immunocompromised nurse is at risk of severe or disseminated infection.
A non-immune staff member would be susceptible and could become infected and spread the virus.
Correct. Only staff with documented immunity (prior disease confirmed by titer or history, or 2 vaccine doses) should care for clients with varicella.
questions.rationale: Varicella is highly contagious by the airborne route. Assign staff with documented immunity. Pregnant, immunocompromised, or non-immune staff should not be exposed.
questions.takeaway: Varicella clients get immune caregivers only.

questions.stem: The nurse is helping an 82-year-old client with dry, thin skin bathe. After performing hand hygiene, which action should the nurse take first?
options: Check that the bath water is lukewarm
Apply a moisturizer to the driest areas of the skin
Wash the skin gently with a mild liquid cleanser
Pat the skin dry with a soft towel
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults have decreased sensation and fragile skin. Checking for lukewarm water first prevents burns and avoids stripping oils from dry skin.
Incorrect. Moisturizer is applied at the end, right after bathing while the skin is still slightly damp, to hold in water.
Incorrect. Washing with a mild cleanser is correct, but the water temperature must be checked before the client's skin is exposed.
Incorrect. Patting dry is correct technique but comes after washing and rinsing.
questions.rationale: Older adults have thin, dry skin with fewer sebaceous glands and decreased sensation, so hot water can burn or dry the skin. Safety comes first: the nurse checks that the water is lukewarm, washes gently with a mild or liquid cleanser, rinses well, pats dry, and applies moisturizer after bathing. Older adults usually bathe every other day rather than daily.
questions.takeaway: Lukewarm water first, then mild cleanser, pat dry, and moisturize.

questions.stem: The school nurse is teaching the parents of a 7-year-old treated with an over-the-counter lice treatment. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Use a fine-tooth nit comb on wet hair to remove nits
Wash bedding and hats in hot water and dry on high heat
Use a cream rinse or conditioner right before applying the lice treatment
Keep your child home from school until every nit is gone
Tell your child not to share combs, brushes, hats, or helmets
Spray the furniture and carpets with an insecticide fogger
optionRationales: Correct. Combing wet hair with a nit comb removes nits and lice that survive treatment.
Correct. Hot water and high-heat drying kill lice and nits on fabric. Items that can't be washed can be sealed in a plastic bag.
Incorrect. Conditioner coats the hair and reduces how well the pediculicide sticks and works.
Incorrect. Children can return to school after treatment starts. Keeping them home until every nit is gone is not needed.
Correct. Lice spread by head-to-head contact and shared personal items.
Incorrect. Fumigant sprays and foggers are not recommended. They can be toxic, and lice don't survive long off the scalp. Vacuuming is enough.
questions.rationale: Lice care combines a pediculicide, mechanical nit removal, hot laundering or bagging of personal items, and not sharing items. Household insecticides and school exclusion until nit-free are not recommended.
questions.takeaway: Lice: treat, comb, hot-wash, don't share. No foggers and no conditioner first.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old wrestler has a 3-cm scaly, ring-shaped patch with a raised border and central clearing on the forearm. Two teammates have similar lesions. Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate to confirm the most likely cause?

Patch testing on the upper back
Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation
Punch biopsy of the lesion border
optionRationales: A Tzanck smear looks for multinucleated giant cells in herpes-virus vesicles.
Patch testing identifies type IV contact allergens.
Correct. KOH dissolves keratin in the skin scraping so fungal hyphae and spores can be seen under a microscope. It confirms tinea.
Biopsy is used to tell benign from malignant lesions. It is not the first test for a suspected fungal infection.
questions.rationale: An annular, scaly patch with central clearing that spreads among athletes in close contact suggests tinea corporis (tinea gladiatorum). Each skin test has a target. KOH detects fungus, Tzanck detects herpes viruses, patch testing detects contact allergy, Wood lamp shows fluorescence (some tinea, vitiligo), and biopsy detects neoplasm.
questions.takeaway: Ringworm → KOH.

questions.stem: A client reports an itchy, red rash with small vesicles on the left wrist that is exactly the shape of the metal watch band she has worn for years. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: Irritant contact dermatitis caused by sweat and soap trapped under the band
Allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to nickel
Tinea corporis spread to the wrist from fungus living on the watch band
Atopic dermatitis triggered by the client's personal history of asthma
optionRationales: Irritant dermatitis is non-immune and usually causes diffuse dryness, burning, and cracking. It does not sharply outline an object.
Correct. A rash that exactly matches the shape of the allergen, with itching and vesicles after sensitization, is typical of allergic contact dermatitis. Nickel is a common cause.
Tinea forms an annular scaly patch with central clearing. It does not match an object's outline.
Atopic dermatitis typically affects flexural areas and is not shaped like a specific contact item.
questions.rationale: Allergic contact dermatitis needs prior sensitization, appears a day or more after re-exposure, and takes the shape of the contact item. It is confirmed by patch testing and managed by avoidance and topical corticosteroids.
questions.takeaway: Rash in the shape of the object = allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.stem: A dental assistant has itchy, red skin with small vesicles on both hands and wrists that ends in a sharp line where her gloves stop. The rash began about 2 days after she started using a new brand of latex gloves. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
